plate_findings.evidence: Transverse ultrasound scan... with the ankle at rest shows the peroneus longus (L) and peroneus brevis, (B) tendons in anatomical position.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (a, b, c). a: Shows the resting, anatomical position of the tendons, providing baseline evidence for evaluation of peroneal tendon dislocation. b: Demonstrates the dynamic subluxation of the tendons during eversion, a primary sign of peroneal tendon dislocation. c: Shows the tendon returning to anatomical position during movement, supporting the dynamic diagnosis of tendon subluxation.
panels.attribution_text: Bureau and Ziegler. Economics of Musculoskeletal Ultrasound.. Current radiology reports 2016. doi:10.1007/s40134-016-0169-5. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Retromalleolar intrasheath peroneal tendon subluxation in a young downhill skier occult at MRI and demonstrated at dynamic ultrasound examination. a Transverse ultrasound scan at the level of the lateral malleolus with the ankle at rest shows the peroneus longus (L) and peroneus brevis, (B) tendons in anatomical position. The arrow points at a mildly thickened superior retinaculum. b During active ankle eversion, the tendons abruptly interchange position within the retromalleolar groove. Note the increased laxity of the superior retinaculum (arrow). c As the ankle is brought into neutral position, the tendons suddenly switched back to their anatomical position. (arrow = superior retinaculum)

in_text_mentions: On admission, physical examination revealed a palpable prominence over the lateral malleolus, as well as tenderness to palpation along the peroneal tendons. A palpable click sensation was noted on resistance to eversion, suggestive of the PT dislocation, which was also visible on the fibula (Fig. 1). Neurological examinations, including sensation, motor function, and vascular assessment, were unremarkable. The preoperative American orthopedic foot and ankle society (AOFAS) score[9] was 56 points (pain: 20 points, function: 26 points, and alignment: 10 points).

in_text_mentions: ignificant tenderness on medial malleolus and little tenderness on lateral malleolus were noted on palpation of the ankle joint. Neurovascular function of the foot and ankle was normal. Radiographs disclosed minimally-displaced fracture of the medial malleolus and a barely visible small avulsion fracture on the posterodistal part of the lateral malleolus (Fig. 1). Computed tomography (CT) scan to determine the exact position of the avulsion fracture of lateral malleolus revealed a flake avulsion of superior peroneal retinaculum (SPR) from the posterior aspect of the lateral malleolus (Fig. 2).
